headline: High risk of shared-filesystem prompt injection and cascading errors; both agents can write the same workspace and execute shell commands by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and Agent A explicitly shares state via filesystem and git while Agent B shares state via filesystem and can read clipboard/files. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge even without a documented parser. The pathway is not provably blocked, but it is less direct than a raw shared MCP channel.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests files from the shared workspace as instructions, injected content can steer actions.
IF either agent treats repository text as trusted prompts, malicious instructions in files can propagate.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic file ingestion for both agents.
Use a read-only handoff file for inter-agent communication.
Require human review before either agent executes instructions from files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, git history, shell environment, and cwd files; Agent B can access the entire user filesystem and clipboard. Because both share filesystem-based state, sensitive local data can flow from A into B’s outputs or vice versa in default setups. The blast radius includes code and local files, so this is more than a low-risk local-only overlap.
conditions: IF either agent writes secrets or sensitive files into the shared workspace, the other can read them.
IF clipboard transfer is used between agents, pasted secrets may be exposed to Agent B.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared directory.
Disable clipboard-based transfer between agents.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Mount only a narrow project subdirectory for each agent.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and git-state modification, and both share state via filesystem. That matches the rubric’s dangerous overlap pattern: concurrent writes to the same mutable workspace can corrupt files or git history without locking. The pair’s defaults make conflict likely and potentially irreversible for repository state.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent commits or rewrites can conflict.
IF either agent writes generated artifacts into shared paths, the other can overwrite them.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable auto-commit or auto-rebase behavior.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce code, shell commands, and file edits; Agent B can also execute shell and write files. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations from A can cascade into destructive actions by B. The pair lacks any documented verification boundary in the profiles, so the safer higher severity is warranted.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A’s commands or patches without verification, mistakes can be executed.
IF Agent A emits incorrect file edits and Agent B applies them, downstream damage can spread.
mitigations: Require B to diff and validate A’s output before execution.
Insert a human approval step for destructive commands.
Limit A to proposal-only mode.
Run both agents on disposable test data first.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A is Anthropic Claude Code with docs-only evidence and handles API keys plus git credentials; Agent B is Open Interpreter with access to the entire user filesystem and model-provider keys. The profiles do not document matching residency, retention, or certification controls, so compliance mismatch is plausible. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of sensitive local and credential data.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in the shared workspace, both agents may process it under undocumented controls.
IF organizational policy requires specific retention or residency guarantees, the profiles do not show them.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace.
Review vendor DPA and retention settings before use.
Use synthetic or redacted data for agent runs.
Restrict both agents to non-regulated projects.
